planting.note: Set container-grown trees in fall into cool, humus-rich soil on a north-facing canyon slope or stream-cut bench where taller pines and oaks break the midday sun. Bare-root transplanting is poorly tolerated because of a deep, slow-forming taproot, so choose the planting site with care from the start.

directions: Arizona madrone grows along the cool, perennial-water canyons of the Chiricahua, Huachuca, and Santa Catalina ranges, usually rooted in the dappled light beneath Chihuahua and ponderosa pine or silverleaf oak rather than in open exposure. Its smooth, reddish, peeling bark and glossy evergreen leaves give it year-round presence, while clusters of small white urn-shaped flowers in spring mature into orange-red berries that mockingbirds and other canyon wildlife seek out in fall. Once its roots are established in well-drained, shaded canyon soil it needs little supplemental irrigation, but it resists transplant far more than young nursery stock and should be sited only once and left undisturbed. It is a slow, long-lived centerpiece for a Southwest canyon-woodland garden built around broken, filtered shade.

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in early summer or set container shrubs in fall beneath canyon-bottom conifers and oaks, where cool, moist, humus-rich soil mimics its native streamside understory. Seed can be fall-sown and left to overwinter outdoors for natural cold stratification, though germination is slow and uneven.

directions: This spiny, arching gooseberry is a shaded-canyon and mixed-conifer understory shrub of the Madrean sky islands of southeastern Arizona and adjacent New Mexico, typically found rooted along cool, humus-rich canyon drainages well above the desert floor. In spring it produces showy pendant flowers in shades of coral, orange, and pink that draw early hummingbirds, followed by bristly, glandular-haired orange-red berries that ripen through summer and are edible once the fine spines are rubbed off. It tolerates considerable drought once established in its native rocky, well-drained soil but performs best with its roots shaded from the hottest afternoon sun, making it a good understory choice beneath a canyon-garden canopy of oak, maple, or pine. Light thinning after fruiting keeps the arching canes from becoming overly tangled.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall along a canyon bench or streambank in deep, cool soil beneath an established sycamore or oak canopy, where this variety naturally occurs as a mid-story tree rather than in open sun. Keep roots consistently moist through the first two growing seasons to mimic the perennial-water drainages where it is found.

directions: Southwestern black cherry occupies the shaded, perennial-stream canyon bottoms of the Madrean sky islands, growing as an understory or mid-canopy tree beneath Arizona sycamore, velvet ash, and canyon live oak rather than as the tall forest-form tree found in the eastern United States. Clusters of small white flowers open along the branches in spring and give way to small, dark, bird-favored cherries by late summer, while the glossy foliage takes on yellow tones before dropping in fall. It is markedly more shade-tolerant and water-loving than the dryland Prunus serotina varieties of the Southwest, reflecting its narrow niche along permanently running canyon streams. As with other black cherry varieties, wilting foliage and pits contain cyanogenic compounds and should be kept away from livestock, though the ripe fruit itself is safe and has traditionally been used for jelly.

planting.note: Direct-sow in spring onto rocky, gravelly soil along a canyon-slope planting bed, or set divisions where the roots will stay cool in dappled shade beneath canyon shrubs and trees. This groundsel self-sows modestly where happy, so allow a little open gravel nearby for volunteers.

directions: New Mexico groundsel grows on the rocky, part-shaded canyon slopes and oak-pine margins of the Madrean sky islands, where it forms low rosettes of deeply cut, cobwebby-haired leaves beneath the broken canopy at the edges of canyon drainages. Clusters of bright yellow daisy-like flowers rise on slender stalks in spring and are a reliable early source of nectar for small native bees and butterflies before most other canyon wildflowers bloom. It thrives in lean, fast-draining rocky soil and actually declines in rich, heavily watered garden beds, making it a good fit for a naturalistic canyon rock garden rather than a conventional border. Once established it needs only occasional supplemental water during extended dry spells.
sources: Native Plant Society of New Mexico

planting.note: Direct-sow or set divisions in spring into cool, humus-rich soil on the true shaded floor of a canyon planting, tucked beneath rock ledges or understory shrubs where it would naturally seed into leaf litter. Keep soil consistently moist through the first season while roots establish in the shade.

directions: Fragrant snakeroot is a true canyon-floor plant of the Madrean sky islands, growing in full shade beneath rock overhangs and dense understory along cool, perennial-water drainages where direct sun rarely reaches the soil. Rounded clusters of small white to pale pink flowers open from late summer into fall, well after most shade perennials have finished, and draw a late surge of butterflies and other pollinators moving through the canyon corridor. Its soft, slightly aromatic foliage spreads gradually by short rhizomes to form a loose groundcover rather than a tight mat, filling gaps between ferns and sedges in a shaded native planting. It performs poorly in hot, open sun and should be reserved for the deepest shade available in a canyon-themed garden.

planting.note: Direct-sow or set divisions in spring along the brighter, partly shaded margins of a canyon planting where seasonal seep moisture lingers into summer. This variety tolerates more shade and less heat than lowland bee balms but still wants several hours of filtered light to flower well.

directions: Mountain bee balm occupies the moister, part-shaded margins of Madrean sky-island canyons, where seasonal seeps and streamside soil let it bridge the gap between open pine-oak slopes and the deep shade of the canyon floor. Its strongly mint-scented foliage and lavender, whorled flower heads open through mid and late summer, drawing a steady stream of native bees, hummingbirds, and butterflies along the canyon corridor. Compared with lowland forms of wild bergamot it holds up better to cool nights and partial canopy, and it is notably more resistant to the powdery mildew that often disfigures bee balm in humid gardens. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain airflow and renew vigorous flowering.
sources: Native Plant Society of New Mexico
